You have two options: **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** for one-way server-to-browser updates, or **WebSockets** for two-way communication.

**SSE (best fit for one-way push)**
SSE is a standard for streaming data from the server to the client over HTTP.[4] It uses the `text/event-stream` format, which is supported natively by browsers with the `EventSource` API[4]. It's commonly used for AI chat streaming, live notifications, logs and observability, and other cases where the server pushes updates to the client.[4] This feature was added in FastAPI 0.135.0.[4]

FastAPI also handles some details for you. It will send a "keep alive" `ping` comment every 15 seconds when there hasn't been any message, to prevent some proxies from closing the connection[3], and it set[s] the `Cache-Control: no-cache` header to prevent caching of the stream[3] and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` to prevent buffering in proxies like Nginx.

The excerpts I have don't include the SSE endpoint code. For that, see the full "Server-Sent Events (SSE)" tutorial page.

**WebSockets (if the browser also needs to send data)**
First, add `websockets` (a Python library that makes it easy to use the "WebSocket" protocol) to your project[2] with `uv add websockets`. Then define an endpoint:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    while True:
        data = await websocket.receive_text()
        await websocket.send_text(f"Message text was: {data}")
```

In the browser, connect with `new WebSocket("ws://localhost:8000/ws")` and handle incoming messages in `ws.onmessage`. You can send (and receive) many messages, and all of them will use the same WebSocket connection.[1]

If you broadcast to several clients using an in-memory list, keep in mind that it will only work while the process is running, and will only work with a single process.[5] For something more robust, supported by Redis, PostgreSQL or others, check encode/broadcaster[5].
